{"sample_id": "blind-6d26a8c8bcd74d88b2b81031f1935bf7", "theorem": "I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "Interpret a final configuration as a maximal collection of pairwise disjoint straight 3-stamp blocks.

For the lower bound, first let n≥2. There are n(n−2) horizontal and n(n−2) vertical triples, hence 2n(n−2) potential triples altogether. Maximality means that every potential triple contains a removed stamp.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal potential triples: their starting positions differ from that of the block by at most two. Its three stamps each meet at most three vertical triples, giving at most nine more. Thus one block meets at most 14 potential triples. The same argument applies to a vertical block. Therefore

14b(n) ≥ 2n(n−2),

so

b(n) ≥ n²/7 − 2n/7.

For n=1, b(1)=0 and the same stated inequality holds. Thus we may take c=2/7.

For the upper bound, consider first the whole infinite square grid. In row r, for every integer k, select the horizontal block whose columns are

5k+r, 5k+r+1, 5k+r+2.

These blocks are pairwise disjoint. In each row the unselected columns occur in runs of only two, so every horizontal triple meets a selected block. Every vertical triple also meets one: if a stamp in row r and column q is unselected, then q−r modulo 5 lies in {3,4}. If three stamps in rows r,r+1,r+2 and column q were all unselected, then, writing x=q−r modulo 5, we would have

x, x−1, x−2 ∈ {3,4},

which is impossible. Hence this infinite periodic packing meets every horizontal and vertical triple.

Now retain only those selected blocks lying completely inside the n×n sheet. In each row there are at most n/5+1 such blocks, so their total number is at most

n²/5+n.

Let S consist of the cells in the first two or last two columns; thus |S|≤4n. We claim that every triple not hit by the retained blocks intersects S. Indeed, the infinite packing hits that triple. If the relevant infinite block was not retained, then it crossed the left or right boundary, and every one of its cells lying in the sheet is in S.

Starting with the retained blocks, greedily tear out any further available block until none remains. Every added block was unhit by the original retained blocks, so it intersects S. Since the added blocks are disjoint, charge each to a distinct cell of S. Consequently at most 4n blocks are added. The resulting configuration is maximal and uses at most

n²/5+n+4n = n²/5+5n

blocks. Therefore b(n)≤n²/5+5n, so d=5 works. Together with the lower bound, this proves the theorem for every positive integer n."}
